title: AAP/NASPGHAN Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Faltering Weight
breakthrough: The first joint AAP and NASPGHAN guideline on the problem formerly called failure to thrive, developed by a multidisciplinary panel working from 2021 to 2024 using GRADE. It replaces the label "failure to thrive" with "faltering weight" and moves diagnosis from percentiles to z-scores. A child meets criteria with any one of: weight-for-length or BMI-for-age below −1.65 z (about the 5th percentile); in a child under 2, weight-gain velocity below −2 z for age (2.3rd percentile); or a decline of 1 z-score or more in weight, weight-for-length or BMI.
impact: The decisive change is the one-z-score decline. Diagnosis no longer waits for a child to reach the 3rd or 5th percentile or to cross two major percentile lines — a single z-score drop is enough, which moves recognition considerably earlier.
practical: Plot z-scores, not percentiles, and act on the trajectory rather than the position. The guideline supports de-escalating reflexive laboratory and imaging workups in favour of structured nutrition assessment, catch-up caloric targets and multidisciplinary feeding evaluation. Note that the terminology change is not cosmetic: "failure to thrive" attributes failure to the child or the parent, and the new label describes an observation.
link: Pediatrics — AAP/NASPGHAN clinical practice guideline for diagnosis and management of faltering weight

verify.status: corrected — the diagnostic thresholds given were from a different classification system
verify.note: The guideline is real and correctly identified: first joint AAP/NASPGHAN CPG, GRADE, panel 2021-2024, Pediatrics 2026;157(4):e2025075764, and it does replace 'failure to thrive' with 'faltering weight' and move from percentiles to z-scores. THE THRESHOLDS ARE WRONG. The submission gives severity bands of mild −1 to −1.9, moderate −2 to −2.9, severe ≤−3. Those are the ASPEN/Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics paediatric MALNUTRITION severity indicators, not this guideline's diagnostic criteria. The guideline's criteria are: weight-for-length or BMI-for-age < −1.65 z; or, under age 2, weight-gain velocity < −2 z; or a decline of ≥1 z-score. A resident applying the submitted bands would use the wrong cut-off in both directions — waiting for −2 before diagnosing, when a 1 z-score decline already qualifies. Corrected, with the one-z-score point moved into the impact field because it is the substantive change and the submission missed it. Date corrected: 2026, not 2025.

title: International Consensus Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock (Phoenix)
breakthrough: The SCCM Pediatric Sepsis Definition Task Force retired the 2005 SIRS-based criteria and derived the Phoenix Sepsis Score from a large international database, systematic review and modified Delphi process. Sepsis in a child under 18 with suspected infection is now a Phoenix score of at least 2 points, indicating potentially life-threatening dysfunction of the respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation or neurological systems. Septic shock is sepsis with at least 1 cardiovascular point — severe hypotension for age, blood lactate above 5 mmol/L, or a need for vasoactive medication.
impact: Anchors the definition to measured organ dysfunction rather than to vital-sign derangements that most febrile children have. The mortality gradient validates it: score ≥2 carried in-hospital mortality of 7.1% in higher-resource and 28.5% in lower-resource settings, more than eight times that of children with suspected infection not meeting criteria; septic shock 10.8% and 33.5% respectively.
practical: Learn the four organ systems and the three cardiovascular triggers, because the cardiovascular point is what separates sepsis from septic shock and therefore what drives escalation. The resource-setting difference in mortality is not a footnote — the same score means a very different prognosis depending on where the child is, which matters when reading literature from another health system.
link: JAMA — international consensus criteria for pediatric sepsis and septic shock

verify.note: Verified and accurate as submitted, including the Phoenix score ≥2 threshold, the four organ systems, and all three cardiovascular criteria for septic shock (severe hypotension for age, lactate >5 mmol/L, vasoactive requirement). Two additions rather than corrections: the date is February 2024, not 2025, and the in-hospital mortality figures have been added because they are what justify the cut-off and the submission omits them. One softening: the submission says the criteria 'significantly reduce false-positive sepsis alarms in pediatric emergency departments and ICUs'. That is the design intent and the direction of separate prospective comparisons against the 2005 criteria, but it is not a finding of the consensus paper itself, so it is not stated as one.

title: Omalizumab for Multiple Food Allergies (OUtMATCH Stage 1)
breakthrough: In stage 1 of this NIH-sponsored randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 180 participants aged 1 to 55 — 177 of them children and adolescents — allergic to peanut and at least two other foods received omalizumab or placebo every two or four weeks for 16 to 20 weeks. 67% met the primary endpoint versus 7% on placebo, meaning they could tolerate a substantially larger quantity of peanut before a moderate-to-severe reaction. Secondary endpoints for cashew, milk and egg improved similarly, across milk, egg, wheat, cashew, hazelnut and walnut. Safety was comparable apart from more injection-site reactions. The FDA approved omalizumab on 16 February 2024 for reducing allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, from accidental exposure in patients aged 1 year and over.
impact: The first pharmacological option that raises the reaction threshold across several foods at once, in children as young as one, without food-specific desensitisation.
practical: Counsel this precisely, because the indication is narrow and easy to overstate. Omalizumab raises the threshold for an accidental exposure; it does not permit deliberate ingestion of the allergen, and strict avoidance and adrenaline autoinjectors continue unchanged. The effect depends on continued dosing — this is ongoing treatment, not a cure or a course, and stopping it removes the protection.
link: NEJM — omalizumab for the treatment of multiple food allergies

verify.status: corrected — 'disease-modifying' is wrong, and the avoidance advice was unsafe
verify.note: The trial is real and the results check out: OUtMATCH stage 1, NEJMoa2312382, 180 participants aged 1-55 (177 children/adolescents), 67% versus 7% on the primary endpoint, FDA approval 16 February 2024. FOUR CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission calls omalizumab 'a disease-modifying monotherapy'. It is not disease-modifying — the FDA indication is reduction of reactions on accidental exposure, the benefit is threshold-raising, and it depends on continued dosing. (2) SAFETY: the submission says it eases 'reliance on strict food avoidance'. It does not. Patients must continue strict avoidance and carry adrenaline; a family told otherwise could feed a child an allergen. That is the most consequential error in this list and the entry now states the opposite explicitly. (3) 'Led to updated AAP and AAAAI allergy guidelines' could not be confirmed; the FDA approval is the verifiable regulatory event and is cited instead. (4) Trial name is OUtMATCH, not OUToMATCH; date 2024, not 2025.

title: Nirsevimab Effectiveness Against RSV ICU Admission and Acute Respiratory Failure
breakthrough: A prospective 27-hospital case-control investigation across 24 states estimated nirsevimab effectiveness at 80% against RSV-associated infant ICU admission and 83% against acute respiratory failure — defined as illness requiring CPAP, bilevel positive airway pressure or invasive mechanical ventilation — with doses received a median of 52 and 50 days before symptom onset respectively.
impact: Confirms the benefit at the severe end of the disease spectrum, which is where a passive-immunisation programme has to prove itself. Most infants in the cohort were previously healthy, so the effect is not confined to the high-risk groups palivizumab was reserved for.
practical: Protection wanes measurably within a single season: 86% effectiveness in the first 7 to 59 days after administration falling to 66% from 60 to 183 days. That is the number that matters for timing — an infant dosed early in the autumn is less protected in a late-peaking season. Supports the CDC/ACIP and AAP recommendation for infants under 8 months entering their first RSV season.
link: Nirsevimab effectiveness against ICU admission for RSV in infants, 24 states, December 2024-April 2025

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, with waning added
verify.note: Verified and accurate as submitted: 80% against RSV-associated ICU admission and 83% against acute respiratory failure, from a prospective 27-hospital case-control investigation across 24 states, December 2024 to April 2025. IMPORTANT ADDITION: effectiveness fell from 86% at 7-59 days to 66% at 60-183 days after administration. The submission presents a single flat figure, which would have a clinician assume uniform season-long protection; the waning is what determines dosing timing and belongs in the entry. Also added that most infants were previously healthy, since that is what distinguishes this from the palivizumab era, and the operational definition of acute respiratory failure so the 83% is interpretable.

title: Whole-Body Hypothermia in Preterm Infants 33 to 35 Weeks with Neonatal Encephalopathy
breakthrough: The NICHD Neonatal Research Network randomised infants of 33 to 35 weeks' gestation with moderate or severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, at under 6 hours of age, to hypothermia at 33.5 °C for 72 hours or normothermia at 37 °C, across 19 centres between July 2015 and December 2022. Death or disability at 18 to 22 months occurred in 35% (29/83) with hypothermia versus 29% (20/69) with normothermia (adjusted relative risk 1.11, 95% credibility interval 0.74 to 2.00). Death occurred in 20% (18/88) versus 12% (9/78), adjusted relative risk 1.38 (0.79 to 2.85). Bayesian analysis with a neutral prior gave a 74% probability of increased death or disability and an 87% probability of increased death with cooling.
impact: This is not merely a null result. The point estimates and the Bayesian probabilities both point towards harm, which is a stronger basis for changing practice than an absence of benefit would be.
practical: Restrict therapeutic hypothermia to infants of 36 weeks' gestation or more, and do not cool a late-preterm infant off-label outside a trial. When explaining the decision to a family, the honest statement is not that cooling was unhelpful but that in the only randomised trial in this gestational range there was an 87% probability that it increased death.
link: JAMA Pediatrics — whole-body hypothermia for neonatal encephalopathy in preterm infants 33 to 35 weeks' gestation

verify.status: matched with corrections — the result is stronger than submitted
verify.note: Verified: NICHD Neonatal Research Network randomised trial, 19 centres, July 2015 to December 2022, infants 33-35 weeks with moderate or severe HIE cooled at under 6 hours, no reduction in death or disability at 18-22 months. The submission is correct as far as it goes but UNDERSTATES the finding. It says cooling 'did not reduce the primary outcome' and mentions 'potential adverse event risks'. The actual data point towards harm: 35% versus 29% for death or disability, 20% versus 12% for death, and a Bayesian analysis giving 74% probability of increased death or disability and 87% probability of increased death. Those figures have been added, because 'no benefit' and 'probably harmful' support different conversations with a family and different institutional policy. The submission's practical conclusion — restrict cooling to ≥36 weeks and avoid off-label use — is right and is kept.

title: Characterizing Long COVID in Children and Adolescents (RECOVER-Pediatrics)
date: 21 August 2024, with a separate young-children analysis since
breakthrough: The NIH RECOVER-Pediatrics observational cohort, over 5,300 participants at more than 60 institutions, identified four distinct symptom clusters in school-age children and three in adolescents. The most predictive symptoms differed by age: in school-age children, trouble with memory or focusing, back or neck pain, abdominal pain, headache, specific fears, school refusal, itchy skin or rash, disturbed sleep, nausea or vomiting and light-headedness; in adolescents, change or loss of smell or taste, body, muscle or joint pain, daytime tiredness or low energy, tiredness after walking, back or neck pain, memory or concentration difficulty, headache and light-headedness. These patterns tracked with worse overall health and quality of life. A separate RECOVER analysis has since described distinct symptom patterns in infants and toddlers.
impact: Establishes that paediatric long COVID is not one syndrome and not the adult syndrome scaled down. School refusal and specific fears sitting among the most predictive symptoms in school-age children is the finding a clinician is least likely to anticipate.
practical: Screen by developmental stage rather than against a single symptom list, and take somatic and behavioural presentations in younger children seriously rather than routing them straight to a psychological explanation. Note that the school-age and adolescent clusters come from the JAMA cohort paper, while the infant and toddler patterns are a separate later analysis — they are not all one publication.
link: JAMA — characterizing long COVID in children and adolescents

verify.status: corrected — two studies were merged into one, and the cluster findings were missing
verify.note: Real: RECOVER-Pediatrics, JAMA, published 21 August 2024, over 5,300 participants at more than 60 institutions. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission describes one study identifying clusters 'across developmental stages, highlighting distinct presentations in infants/toddlers versus older children and teens'. The JAMA cohort paper covers school-age children and adolescents; the infant and toddler patterns are a SEPARATE later RECOVER analysis. Merging them attributes findings to a paper that does not contain them. (2) The actual structure — four clusters in school-age children, three in adolescents — was absent from the submission, along with the symptom lists, which are the usable content. Both added. Date corrected to 2024. The submission's example symptoms ('post-exertional malaise and dysautonomia in teens') are plausible but were not among the most predictive symptoms reported, so the published lists are used instead.

title: Fluoride Exposure and Children's IQ Scores: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
breakthrough: A meta-analysis of 74 cross-sectional and prospective cohort studies published between 1989 and 2023 found an inverse association between fluoride exposure and children's IQ. In the 13 studies with individual-level exposure measures, IQ was 1.63 points lower per 1 mg/L increase in urinary fluoride. The association persisted when restricted to the 22 high-quality studies and was consistent across subgroups by sex, age, country, outcome measure, exposure timing and exposure matrix, including at exposures below 1.5 mg/L.
impact: Moved a contested literature into a mainstream paediatric journal with a quantified effect estimate, and prompted an unusually public methodological argument — a JAMA Pediatrics editorial urging caution, published critiques, and a formal response from the authors.
practical: The context that makes this interpretable is missing from most summaries: the 74 studies were conducted in 10 countries and none in the United States, and 52 of them were rated high risk of bias. Most exposures studied are well above the 0.7 mg/L used in US community water fluoridation. The defensible clinical response is to total up a child's systemic fluoride — water source, supplements, swallowed toothpaste — before adding a systemic supplement, while continuing topical fluoride, which is where the caries benefit lies and which this analysis does not address.
link: JAMA Pediatrics — fluoride exposure and children's IQ scores: a systematic review and meta-analysis

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, with the contested context restored
verify.note: Verified: JAMA Pediatrics January 2025, 74 studies from 1989-2023, inverse association, effect estimate of −1.63 IQ points per 1 mg/L urinary fluoride in the 13 individual-level studies, association persisting below 1.5 mg/L in high-quality evidence. THREE ADDITIONS, all of which change how a pediatrician should use this. 52 of the 74 studies were rated high risk of bias and only 22 high quality. The studies were done in 10 countries and NONE in the United States, at exposures generally well above the 0.7 mg/L of US community fluoridation. And the paper drew a substantial published critique, including a JAMA Pediatrics editorial counselling caution — a clinician quoting the headline as settled will be met with it. ONE CORRECTION: the submission says the study 'prompted public health and pediatric dental organizations to re-examine total daily fluoride thresholds'. I could not confirm an organisational threshold review, so it is not asserted; the practical advice about totalling systemic exposure while continuing topical fluoride is sound and is kept.

title: Residual Exacerbations on Mepolizumab in Urban Children with Asthma (MUPPITS-2)
journal: The Lancet (parent trial) and Nature Communications (mechanism)
breakthrough: MUPPITS-2 randomised urban children with exacerbation-prone eosinophilic asthma to mepolizumab added to guidelines-based care, and found a 27% relative reduction in severe exacerbations over 12 months, concentrated in the autumn. Nasal airway transcriptomics then showed what mepolizumab does and does not switch off: correlation among eosinophil-specific genes was lost, but correlation among mast-cell-specific genes, type 2 cytokines and airway epithelial inflammatory genes was conserved and in places strengthened. A separate analysis found activated sputum eosinophils still associated with exacerbations in treated children.
impact: Explains why a biologic that works does not work completely. Depleting eosinophils does not dismantle the wider type 2 network or the epithelial inflammatory programme, and exacerbation risk persists through both.
practical: Do not withdraw controller therapy because a child is on a biologic: continue inhaled corticosteroid and reliever therapy, and treat autumn viral season as the high-risk window it demonstrably is. The honest framing for a family is a roughly one-quarter reduction in severe exacerbations, not their elimination. Be careful with the shorthand that breakthrough attacks are 'non-type 2' — mast-cell and type 2 cytokine networks were preserved on treatment, and activated eosinophils were still implicated, so residual type 2 activity is part of the picture rather than absent from it.
link: Nature Communications — mepolizumab alters gene regulatory networks of nasal airway type-2 and epithelial inflammation in urban children with asthma

verify.status: corrected — the mechanism is not the clean non-type-2 story submitted
verify.note: Real work, correctly identified: MUPPITS-2 in The Lancet (2022, 27% relative reduction in severe exacerbations, autumn-predominant) with the nasal transcriptomic analysis in Nature Communications (2025, PMID 40897727). CORRECTION TO MECHANISM. The submission says breakthrough exacerbations 'were driven by non-Type 2 inflammatory pathways (specifically epithelial hypersecretion and viral macrophage responses)'. The published finding is subtler and partly the opposite: mepolizumab dissolved eosinophil gene correlation but CONSERVED and sometimes strengthened correlation among mast-cell genes, type 2 cytokines and epithelial inflammatory genes, and a separate JACI analysis found activated sputum eosinophils still associated with exacerbations. So residual type 2 activity persists rather than being replaced by a purely non-T2 process. The specific pathways named in the submission were not confirmed and are not asserted. The submission's clinical conclusion — keep controller therapy, do not rely on the biologic alone — is right and is kept, with the 27% figure added so the magnitude is visible.

title: Exagamglogene Autotemcel: Long-Term Outcomes in Sickle Cell Disease and Beta-Thalassemia
journal: NEJM (pivotal trials) and Blood / ASH (long-term follow-up)
breakthrough: Final results of CLIMB SCD-121: 46 patients with severe sickle cell disease and a mean 4.2 vaso-occlusive crises per year at baseline received exa-cel, an ex vivo CRISPR-Cas9 edited autologous therapy that reactivates fetal haemoglobin. At a median follow-up of 41.3 months, 45 of 45 evaluable patients were free of vaso-occlusive crises and of hospitalisation for them, with a mean crisis-free duration of 35.3 months. Neutrophil engraftment occurred at a median of 27 days and platelet engraftment at 35 days. Durable benefit now extends beyond 5 years in both transfusion-dependent thalassaemia and sickle cell disease.
impact: Establishes gene editing as a durable option that does not require a donor, removing both the matched-donor bottleneck and the risk of graft-versus-host disease.
practical: Read the population before calling this a paediatric result: this cohort was 12 adolescents and 34 adults with a mean age of 21.4 years, and the original approval was for patients aged 12 and over. Transfusion independence is the endpoint in the thalassaemia trial and crisis-freedom in the sickle cell trial — two different trials, not one composite result. The therapy requires myeloablative busulfan conditioning, which brings its own toxicity, infertility risk and need for a specialist centre.
link: NEJM — exagamglogene autotemcel for severe sickle cell disease

verify.status: corrected — presented as a paediatric result from a mostly adult cohort
verify.note: The efficacy data are real and if anything stronger than submitted: CLIMB SCD-121 final results show 45 of 45 evaluable patients crisis-free and hospitalisation-free at a median 41.3 months' follow-up, mean crisis-free duration 35.3 months, with durable benefit beyond 5 years across both indications. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) POPULATION: the submission describes outcomes 'in pediatric patients'. The cohort was 12 adolescents and 34 adults, mean age 21.4 years, and the label at the time covered ages 12 and over — this is not a young-children result, which is the separate 2026 trial. (2) The submission merges vaso-occlusive crisis freedom and transfusion independence into one finding; they are endpoints of two different trials in two different diseases. (3) 'Restructured pediatric hematology guidelines to position autologous gene therapy as a curative therapeutic pathway' overstates what was confirmed; the durable-benefit data and the removal of the donor requirement are stated instead, with busulfan conditioning, infertility risk and centre requirements named because the submission mentions conditioning only in passing.

title: Closing the Evidence Gap for Drugs in Children: Strengthening the Pediatric Research Equity Act
breakthrough: An analysis of how PREA is actually working found that only 28% of the pediatric trials required for drugs approved between 2015 and 2021 had been completed by May 2024. As of 2023 the FDA had granted more than 700 extensions to pediatric study deadlines and classified 250 studies as delayed. Rare-disease designations exempt close to half of new drugs from pediatric testing altogether. Proposed reforms, including the Innovation in Pediatric Drugs Act, would remove the rare-disease exemption.
impact: Quantifies why so much paediatric prescribing remains off-label two decades after the legislation that was supposed to fix it. The exemption, not the requirement, is doing most of the work.
practical: The clinical consequence is the one paediatricians already live with: dosing by extrapolation for years after a drug reaches adults. Note that the reforms described are legislative proposals, not enacted requirements — nothing currently obliges a sponsor to run phase 3 paediatric trials before adult approval, and citing that as existing policy would be wrong.
link: NEJM — closing the evidence gap for drugs in children: measures to strengthen the Pediatric Research Equity Act

verify.status: corrected — proposals described as accomplished policy, and the figures were missing
verify.note: Real: NEJM Perspective, NEJMp2518278, PMID 42012006, published April 2026 (not 2025 — the date is corrected in the field but the entry is left on the submitted year, as with other out-of-year citations in this project). TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission says the piece 'Accelerated FDA and international regulatory initiatives REQUIRING sponsors to initiate Phase 3 pediatric trials prior to adult product approval and remove orphan-drug exemptions'. Those are proposals — the Innovation in Pediatric Drugs Act among them — not enacted requirements, and a resident citing them as current regulation would be wrong. Reworded. (2) The substance was absent: 28% of required trials completed, over 700 deadline extensions, 250 studies delayed, and rare-disease designation exempting nearly half of new drugs. Those figures are the argument and have been added.
